title: Qualified Charitable Distributions (QCDs) — the most efficient give-while-alive vehicle at 70½+
summary: Direct IRA-to-charity transfer that satisfies the RMD, bypasses AGI inflation, and avoids the standard-vs-itemize comparison entirely.
detailsHtml:
The mechanics

IRC §408(d)(8) permits IRA owners age 70½+ to direct annual distributions of up to $111,000 (2026 indexed) directly from a Traditional IRA to a qualifying public 501(c)(3) charity. The distribution is excluded from gross income, counts toward the year's RMD obligation, and bypasses both the AGI inflation that drives IRMAA tier crossings and the §170(b) AGI-based deduction caps. Note the age trigger is the legacy 70½ figure — not the current RMD age of 73. Congress preserved 70½ as the QCD-eligibility entry in both SECURE Act and SECURE 2.0 even as it raised the RMD age.

Why it dominates other charitable vehicles for retirees

A 75-year-old with a $50,000 RMD and an annual charitable habit of $20,000 saves materially by routing the $20K as a QCD rather than as a personal donation. The QCD reduces AGI (lowering IRMAA tier exposure, the percentage of Social Security that's taxable, and Medicare premium calculations), counts toward the RMD, and produces the tax benefit without requiring the household to itemize at all. For a retiree taking the standard deduction (the modal case post-TCJA), a personal cash donation produces zero federal tax benefit while a QCD of the same amount delivers the full income-exclusion value.

The constraints worth knowing

Cannot route to a Donor-Advised Fund (the most common DIY-charity vehicle) or to most private foundations. Must go from the IRA trustee directly to the charity — a personal check from the IRA distribution proceeds doesn't qualify; the distribution must never touch the owner's hands. SECURE 2.0 §307 added a one-time $55,000 (2026 indexed) QCD-to-CRT or charitable gift annuity option, useful for retirees who want a partial income stream from the gift.

Sequencing note. For charitably-inclined retirees with both Traditional IRA balances and a give-while-alive philosophy (see the Zeitgeist: Lifestyle Die-with-Zero treatment), QCDs generally dominate DAF funding, direct cash giving from after-tax dollars, and bunching strategies on the after-tax-result-per-dollar-donated math. The DAF is still useful for pre-70½ donors and for retirees who want grant-making flexibility deferred over years; the QCD is the right tool for retirees making direct annual gifts to operating charities.
